implementation_notes: ISO C has no destructors and no scope-exit hook, so the scope-bound release is a convention: acquire at the top of the function, send every failure path through one `goto out;`, and unlock exactly once at the `out:` label. This is the portable realization and the one that works on every C compiler; its discipline is enforced by review, not by the language.
pitfalls: Any `return` between the lock and the `out:` label leaks the lock and the compiler will not warn.
New failure paths added by maintenance must be routed to the label; that is the same maintenance risk the pattern removes elsewhere.
Early exits that must return a value need the value carried in a variable, which is easy to get wrong when the label is shared.

variants.name: Single-exit goto ladder (portable)

This is the portable realization and the one that works on every C compiler; its discipline is enforced by review, not by the language.

New failure paths added by maintenance must be routed to the label; that is the same maintenance risk the pattern removes elsewhere.

variants.name: POSIX cancellation cleanup stack
variants.implementation_notes: POSIX threads offer a real scope-bound mechanism: pthread_cleanup_push registers a handler that runs when the thread is cancelled or calls pthread_exit, and pthread_cleanup_pop(1) runs the same handler on the normal path - register pthread_mutex_unlock as the handler and the mutex is released on cancellation-driven unwinding, which the goto ladder cannot do. Use it for critical sections in cancellable threads; note the macros must be lexically paired inside one block.
variants.code_sketch:
pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
pthread_cleanup_push(unlock_cleanup, &mutex);  /* handler registered */
...                                            /* critical section    */
pthread_cleanup_pop(1);                        /* release on exit too */
pitfalls: push and pop are macros that expand to an opening and closing brace: they must appear in the same block, cannot be split across functions, and cannot be conditionally unbalanced.
The handler covers cancellation and pthread_exit, not a plain `return` - mixing the cleanup stack with early returns still leaks the lock.
Cancellation can arrive between the lock and the push, so the acquisition order matters (lock first, then push).

variants.name: GCC/Clang cleanup attribute (RAII emulation)
variants.implementation_notes: GCC and Clang accept `__attribute__((cleanup(fn)))` on a local variable: the function runs when the variable goes out of scope, including through return, break and goto. Declaring a dummy variable that points at the mutex gives C the closest thing to RAII - a release that survives every path, including early returns that the cleanup stack does not cover. It is a compiler extension, so restrict it to codebases that already target GCC/Clang on all platforms.
pitfalls: The attribute is a GNU extension: MSVC, strict ISO-C modes and some embedded toolchains reject it, so the portable default stays the goto ladder.
The cleanup callback's parameter type is unchecked; a mismatched pointer is undefined behaviour rather than a compile error.
setjmp/longjmp out of the block and _exit bypass the cleanup entirely.
